subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND SECRECY PROVISIONS TO FILES AND RECORDS

speakeroldname: Mr. E. J. Broome (Vancouver South) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND SECRECY PROVISIONS TO FILES AND RECORDS
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-68, to amend the Juvenile Delinquents Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND SECRECY PROVISIONS TO FILES AND RECORDS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND SECRECY PROVISIONS TO FILES AND RECORDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, section 12 of the Juvenile Delinquents Act sets out the requirement that trials of children shall take place without publicity and separately and apart from the trials of adults. The act prohibits newspapers and all other publications published anywhere in Canada from publishing the names or disclosing the identity of anyone being prosecuted under the Juvenile Delinquents Act. The act therefore provides for secrecy in regard to the actual trial or hearing, but it does not provide this same secrecy in regard to the files and records respecting the trial.
The purpose of this bill is to extend the secrecy provisions of the act to these files and records, and to provide further that these records and files shall be destroyed after a period of five years from the date of the hearing or trial, if no new trial respecting such child or juvenile has taken place during the said period of five years.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in introducing the second reading of Bill No. C-67, an act to amend the Pension Act, I am sure all members will wish to proceed with the second reading stage as expeditiously as possible in view of the fact that we had a lengthy discussion at the resolution stage and in view of the fact that as the bill is an amending bill it deals with a number of particulars which can be more readily discussed in committee. There is also the fact that after second reading of the bill it is my intention to move that the bill be referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs so the members of that committee may examine it in all its details and have available to them the expert advice of officials of the department in case there are any matters that require further explanation.
Without discussing the various segments of the bill I might, however, emphasize that its main purpose is to increase the pensions that are being paid to disabled veterans. I will just indicate the extent of the support which our country is giving the men who suffered disability in wartime. Reading from the annual report of the Department of Veterans Affairs for the fiscal year 1959-60, page 73, I note that for world war I the number of people drawing disability pensions as of March 31, 1960 was 47,845, and their dependents numbered 14,812. The total on the rolls for world war I is 62,657. In so far as world war II is concerned, the number drawing disability pension is 104,911 and their dependents number 17,546, for a total of 122,457.
The annual liability as of March 31, 1960 for both wars was $144,899,781. It might be of interest to the house to put on Hansard the figures with regard to service in the first and second world wars as well as Korea, and indicate the number who became pensioners as a result of these wars. The number who served in world war I totalled 619,636 men and women. Of these 110,000 became pensioners, and of these pensioners 56,002 have since died and 46,482 are still on the pension rolls. In so far as world war II was concerned there were 1,086,343 men and women who served. Of these, 124,401 became pensioners and 11,338 of these pensioners have since died,

leaving 105,294 who are still receiving pensions. In so far as the Korean war is concerned there were 26,791 men and women who served. Of these, 2,032 became pensioners and 49 of these pensioners have since died, leaving 1,636 who are still receiving pensions.
Each year the pension commission, pursuing a constant task, has found it necessary to add people to the pension rolls. During the fiscal year 1959-60, 219 new pensions were awarded to veterans of world war I; 1,981 new pensions were awarded to veterans of world war II and 62 new pensions were awarded to veterans of the Korean war. Of course each year the number who die and pass off the pension rolls increases. So far as world war I veterans are concerned, they are passing off the pension rolls now at the rate of about 2,500 per year.
The problem, however, continues and will continue for many years, and the financial obligation undertaken by the people of Canada is as I have indicated. It was a larger burden on the country some years ago when our population was smaller. In 1930 the financial obligation for pensions was about 9 per cent of the total government expenditures. In 1960, with the great increase in government income and the great increase in government expenditures, the pension commitment represented 2 per cent of total government expenditures.
The bill before us, Mr. Speaker, indicates an increase of approximately $30 million. It deals with all categories who come on the pension rolls, graduated according to the percentage of disability from 100 per cent down to 10 per cent. The bill deals also with the dependents of pensioners and with additional pensions for children. It would be improper, perhaps, to deal in detail with each one of the changes that have been made in. these various categories. This can be done in committee. The bill as printed indicates quite clearly the new scale of pensions and gives a comparison with the old scale. Most of our pensioners are below the 50 per cent rating but there are, of course, large numbers who are in the heavier disability classes from 50 per cent up to 100 per cent.
We hope that through this measure the payments to our disability pensioners will be kept somewhat in accord with the general increase in the cost of living that has occurred over the years, and that they will be placed in a position where they are able to look after themselves, as they all want to do, without being dependent upon other sources for support.
As I mentioned yesterday, the contribution made by our disabled pensioners has been great. They will carry a burden all their lives from the service they performed, and the
Pension Act
people of Canada try to compensate them in part for some of that burden by the pensions that have been in operation over the years and by the increases which we are now presenting to the house.
I hope the house will accept the suggestions in this bill, examine it with care in the standing committee and in committee of the whole when the bill comes back to the house, and pass it as early as is conveniently possible. Then the bill can go to the other place for consideration. I commend Bill No. C-67 to the consideration of the house, and I hope it will meet with general approval.

speechtext:
I wish to make a few brief observations on the bill. As the minister said, this bill to amend the Pension Act has as its main purpose the increasing of disability pensions. The representations recently made to the government by the Canadian Legion recommended that the rates payable under schedules A and B of the Pension Act be increased so that pensioners will regain the position of equality of income, as compared with custom guards, cleaners, helpers and army privates, that was in effect in 1920. In order to achieve that objective the Canadian Legion suggested that a 33J per cent increase in disability pensions would be required.
However, in the bill we notice that the increase is only approximately 20 per cent. That figure is considerably below what the Legion and other organizations thought was necessary at this time in order to compensate veterans and their dependents for the increase in the cost of living and bring them more into line with the increase in wages and so on.
In that connection I would say this. While I am sure the increase will be welcomed by veterans and their dependents across Canada and by members of this House of Commons, it nevertheless falls considerably short, shall I say, of the amount sought by the veterans organizations and of the expectations raised in view of the use of the word "substantial". Of course, Mr. Chairman, that is a relative term. The word "substantial" can mean different things depending on whether you are on the paying end or on the receiving end of any question. It can have different meanings to different people, of course.
I also noticed that in the bill there are a number of other amendments which I am sure will be welcomed by the veterans organizations and by the veterans and their dependants. They are useful and purposeful amendments. However, there again we notice that a number of amendments recommended by the Canadian Legion, the national council of veterans and other veterans organizations have been, shall I say, overlooked. To that extent I presume there will be some disappointment.
When the minister was speaking I listened most attentively, as I usually do to the Minister of Veterans Affairs when he is speaking on veterans affairs. He mentioned that

the percentage of the national income that was required to meet the obligations to veterans in Canada in 1930 was about 9 per cent, if I heard him correctly.

That was my mistake; I should have said 9 per cent of the national expenditure. He also stated that the amount required in 1960 was about 2 per cent of the national expenditure. This clearly indicates that while there has been an enormous increase in our production, in tax collection and consequently in national expenditure, apparently the financial responsibility accepted by the federal government for the veterans and their welfare has declined to a considerable extent in percentage since 1930.
Therefore we must remember that in 1930, in the depression years, the government was able to afford 9 per cent of the national expenditure, according to the minister. We spent, in 1960, only 2 per cent. I think that is a rather good argument in support of the representations made by the Legion and other veterans organizations for the increase they requested. I think it is at least a clear illustration of the modest demands made by the Canadian Legion and of their responsible approach to this problem at this time.
During his remarks the minister paid to the veterans of Canada a tribute which we all heartily endorse. I will say little more at this time. I am going to conclude these few brief remarks because the minister has said that the bill is going to the veterans affairs committee, where the veterans organizations will have an opportunity to make their representations and their points and the members of the committee will have an opportunity to ask questions. I am sure that as in the past, as all members of the committee regardless of party have the interests of the veterans at heart, there will be the usual close study of this legislation and serious consideration of the representations made by representatives of the veterans organization. There is therefore, in my opinion, no occasion for a lengthy debate on the motion for second reading of this bill at this time.

their own country. On reading what the hon. member put on Hansard I recollected the circumstances very well indeed. I admit that I was somewhat irritated by the reply I received at that time, but that problem, of course, has been very largely rectified.

Mr. Speaker, I have been very interested in following the debate of this matter for the last two or three days. I am impressed by the statements that have been made by hon. members on both sides of the house and the support that has been given to the legislation we now have before us.
But I am concerned about one matter. I am very concerned about something that happened earlier this day that would indicate that it may not be advantageous for the members of the house, for the members of the veterans affairs committee, or for the organizations that are interested in veterans affairs to have in the bill this clause which indicates that the act will only become law the first of the month following the passing of the bill. I would suggest that the government should amend this so that the bill will come into force on the day of first reading. If this is not done, it seems to me that the committee is going to be working against the end of February as a deadline to see that all readings of this bill are given prior to that date so this date of March 1 can be the qualifying date.

Pension Act
I suggest that this may be the result. It may not, but it may and therefore I think it is a bad thing if it prevents any organization making the full representation that they may wish to make in relation to any segment of this legislation. I am aware of the requests that have been made by many of the organizations, and I am aware that this bill does not completely satisfy those requests.
While I agree that it is more than people can expect-when they ask for something, they do not necessarily always expect to get it-I think they do expect the opportunity of preparing an argument to indicate that they would like, and for good reasons, more to be done than is being done, no matter how much that may be.
It is for this reason that I hope the government will give serious consideration to withdrawing that clause which puts a deadline in the bill, and will put in a very simple clause which would mean that this legislation would be retroactive to the day of first reading. If the government does not see fit to do that then there may be other methods open to me as a private member to try to accomplish it.
But I would strongly urge the government to eliminate any unpleasantness that may have arisen and any fear that may have been indicated in people's minds, that if the deadline of the end of this month were not met it would produce hardship and would eliminate the payment of the increase in pensions which the veterans need very, very badly. Also, this would afford full discussion in committee and other stages of this bill.

speechtext:
I should like to make a few observations before this item is passed, and I should like to preface my remarks on this important and vital subject with a brief quotation from an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail of January 31, 1951. I shall use it as a text, because it wraps up the whole question in just a few words which I should like to see transcribed in large letters and placed, preferably, on the wall of the office of the minister of immigration. I quote:
What Canada needs is a vigorous immigration policy, selective in the sense that it encourages those who are most likely to take advantage of the opportunities which Canada offers. These will not necessarily be persons who come here to work in a particular trade or profession; they will include persons of energy and initiative who are ready to build a new career in Canada by enterprise and hard work.
According to the Toronto Telegram, our present Prime Minister made the following statement on April 26, 1957:
Increased population was required if Canada's development was to keep pace with her vast resources. A Conservative government would apply a vigorous immigration policy in co-operation with the provinces. The Immigration Act would be overhauled-"Canada must populate or perish''.
That is a noble statement, and it is one which people who are devoid of prejudice

and who have at heart the interests of Canada and her development will, indeed, applaud. The people of Canada gave the right hon. gentleman a mandate to do just that, among other things which I intend to mention today, but nearly four years have gone by and no one has seen a vigorous immigration policy put into effect, nor have we seen a glimpse of the overhaul, so long promised, of the Immigration Act.
What did we see? It will be recalled that actions to restrict immigration were among the first acts of this administration when it took office in June, 1957. The right hon. gentleman's principal minister, that is the Minister of Finance, made the following observations in the course of the budget debate in 1958 and I quote:
Population growth itself does not ensure progress, but in a country the size of ours it has a special significance. It provides a greater market for our agricultural produce and for the products of our factories and reduces vulnerability to changes in external demand. It brings us a greater diversity of talent and the means to employ it to better advantage. It reduces the per capita cost of supplying excellent services in this great land. There can be no doubt that the population growth of the post-war period has had these effects.
If the minister meant what he said, then I would assume he was not in favour of the restrictive measures which were imposed at that time. Now I come to what the minister responsible for immigration has been saying. Bless her heart, I rather like her. The hon. lady's heart was, no doubt, set on introducing changes to the act long before this, but I suspect that restraining influences have upset her earlier intentions which, indeed, have run very much counter to her frequently expressed conviction that unemployment is not increased by bringing immigrants into this country. Last year, during discussion of the estimates of her department the hon. lady promised a thorough revision of the Immigration Act but declared she was anxious not to bring in a half baked piece of legislation which would not stand the test of time. I wonder if this proposed legislation is about burned out?
At the present time Canada's immigration policy, if one can call it a policy, is based on a premise composed of two factors; first, the employment situation at a given time and, second, the racial composition of the country. In practical terms the present regulations mean that the government controls the flow of immigration from year to year and from month to month in accordance with estimates of the economic climate while at the same time favouring immigrants from certain countries. I think this is an unworkable and discriminatory practice, in addition to being unrealistic.
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
How can we reconcile declarations against racial discrimination with what is happening in Canada today when, in actual practice, though we do not reject people on an individual basis, we follow a policy of discrimination against whole nations? It is a policy which is indeed hard to explain, especially to friends in Asiatic countries. Take for instance, the case of Chinese refugees. That of the Japanese is not better. By and large these people make excellent citizens. Most of them are noted for their almost unimpeachable character. A few months ago I came across a news item which dealt with a tribute to a Chinese who ran for alderman in the city of Calgary. He topped the polls and no one will be surprised if in the future he is elected mayor.
Contributions in specialized fields have been made by countless newcomers from many lands. Take, for instance, the case of Mr. Ernest Hakka, an immigrant who came to Canada from Finland eight years ago. Since his arrival here he has invented a machine which will melt snow off city streets for 60 cents a ton, which ordinarily would cost $12 per ton to remove by truck. An appreciable number of Japanese live in Fort William and surrounding districts. It is a matter of record that their conduct as citizens is well above the average, and we could do with more of them. In an interview in Winnipeg two or three months ago the minister made the statement that:
-fears of rising unemployment this winter will not influence the federal government to cut back its immigration program.
She then proceeded to say that:
-every winter the government does its best to persuade immigrants not to come here during the winter.
I wonder what the hon. lady meant by persuasion? If she had said that immigrants were not allowed to come in the winter it would have been a statement closer to the facts. We have the government immigration policy for this winter, at any rate. Simply stated it appears to be a policy of not discouraging immigrants from coming to Canada. The government is just discouraging them, period.
The country needs a policy to encourage immigration rather than to discourage it. It is a matter of record that periods of peacetime prosperity and least unemployment have invariably been identified with a high flow of immigrants. The United States began a vigorous immigration program at a time when that country was poor and backward. The people they brought in without the restrictions and red tape now in use brought about
1940	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the great wealth and power which the republic to the south now enjoys. The same story is being repeated today in Australia.
West Germany, comparatively small in territorial size and very densely populated, received an influx of more than 9 million refugees from eastern Europe in a period of just a few years after the war and the flow is still continuing at a rate of more than
200,000	a year. Yet, notwithstanding the addition of this great number of destitute people, these immigrants turned out to be one of Germany's major assets in the rapid recovery of that country. Today the living standard of West Germany is higher than it has ever been and unemployment is practically non-existent.
I have often expressed the conviction that we are losing a good bet when we ignore the advantage of admitting immigrants who will settle on the land. On previous occasions I have indicated the success which several Dutch families have made in farming in the district of Thunder bay. As population increases and as more and more people flock to urban centres the need for an expansion of agriculture will become apparent.
Every person or family who will undertake to work and develop land suitable for agriculture-extensive tracks of virgin land are available, in my constituency, at least- will not only be choosing a sane and profitable way of life but will also be conferring a benefit on Canada, and since so few native born Canadians will take up farming as their life's work the only answer is to bring in willing hands, farm people from as many countries as possible and as many of them as can be induced to come.
Canada has the potential to handle at least a quarter of a million newcomers every year for an indefinite period of time. Let us now lay the foundation for a worth-while immigration policy which will give our country the shot in the arm she sorely needs.
According to the minister's recent pronouncement, future immigrants are to be selected according to skills and education. The minister has since denied having made that statement and her denial has been accepted. Immigration officials nevertheless appear mainly to favour university graduates. The forefathers of most Canadians came to Canada with anything but university degrees; indeed, they come with few skills and for the most part the degrees they carried were those of qualified hard workers.
It is true, of course, that with the present advance in technology, heavy physical work is no longer the predominant occupation of our labour force but if we are going to open up our northern frontiers-more popularly known as the northern vision-we will need


many hardy pioneers of a fibre which will stand up to northern hardships. It will be easier to attract newcomers to these areas than it will be to find among our native Canadians the necessary number of people to develop the north.
Premier Frost of Ontario speaking to the good roads association annual meeting on October 20, 1960 said in part:
Canada is only at her beginning of opportunity and a greater and more useful population is essential to this country if these opportunities are to be developed.
At this point I should congratulate the minister on the excellent address which she delivered on January 26, 1961 to the Winnipeg real estate board on the subject "How the Immigrants Are Helping Canada".

speechtext:
I gather from the applause that other hon. members have already read the statement but if there are hon. members of this committee who have not read the address, a copy of which was furnished to me, I commend it to their attention because it is a good document and my unreserved congratulations are extended to the minister.
In addition to the pertinent facts pointed out by the minister in her address concerning the contribution to Canada made by immigrants I wish to add a word about the tremendous purchasing power which our new Canadians have infused into the Canadian economy. Newcomers to our shores since 1946 have created a new market equal to a city of the size of metropolitan Toronto. I venture to say that the success of many businesses in the future may well rest in large measure upon their ability to attract these new customers, especially since these new arrivals happen to be in the age group of buyers who make large expenditures. According to reliable estimates 282,164 men, women and children from 50 different countries were admitted to Canada in 1957 which was the greatest year of immigration since 1913. These immigrants created in one single year a consumer demand of approximately $200 million.
The eventual need for motor vehicles and household appliances in one single year may exceed, in round figures, 60,000 automobiles,
70.000	radios, 60,000 washing machines, 60,000 refrigerators, 60,000 sewing machines,
40.000	vacuum cleaners, 30,000 electric stoves, 30,000 television sets, 20,000 oil furnaces, 12,000 coal and coke furnaces, 4,000 gas stoves and 4,000 home freezers, to say nothing of the need for housing which will give a great boost to the housing industry. Each of these people creates a demand for new housing.

You will agree, Mr. Chairman, that this is an impressive list of consumer goods running into many millions of dollars and employing thousands of people in producing them. These are, I repeat, estimated requirements of only one year's influx of immigrants, and there is every reason to expect that this market will be renewed year after year. Unfortunately the only immigrants allowed into the country since 1959 were, with some exceptions, mainly dependents who joined relatives already established here and some workers who came over to take sponsored employment.
The present selective system is not designed to populate and develop Canada. When a government rejects willing and healthy persons it is becoming too selective with the inevitable result that it will retard the economic expansion needed now more than ever to re-establish a climate of confidence and prosperity in the country.
Economists have been saying that there is no connection between immigration and unemployment. A recent analysis of immigration and unemployment made by the Canadian Labour Congress established the opinion that immigration cannot be considered a factor in the present high unemployment situation. In other words, it discounts the notion that today's unemployment is the result of the number of immigrants admitted in recent years. This is an important admission by labour since some of their pronouncements in the past have not been too favourable to immigration.
I was very much interested in what the minister had to say last night about her policy of flexibility in view of the rigid formula of the present act and her statement that before long amendments to the act will be introduced. Her flexible attitude on the interpretation of the present regulations is very commendable, and I would urge that this flexibility be extended to allow prospective brides of Canadian citizens, which brides live in European or Asiatic countries, to be admitted without undue delay. I have known of cases in my own constituency where long delays have caused considerable distress to young people in love and, as you know, lovers are a rather impatient lot.
I listened with more than passing interest to the valuable suggestions made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, a former minister of citizenship and immigration, who on occasion does not hesitate to admit mistakes made under the act relative to restrictions when he occupied that position and who has also stated that immigrants admitted from nearly every country in the world
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration and their descendants have made their contribution to Canada as good Canadians. That was a really fine statement.
I have indicated at various times that I favour a more generous and positive immigration policy but I wish to point out that at no time have I advocated an open door policy. However, the need for revision of our thinking with regard to the number of new citizens Canada can absorb in each calendar year should be quite in order. The basis for selecting a new immigrant should not be national origin or academic accomplishments, desirable though they may be, but rather his character and willingness to work. I wish to conclude my brief remarks with another short quotation from the editorial page of the often quoted Globe and Mail- It is in these words:
What Canada offers today Is room and scope for the person of adventurous ambition, and we shall not select them-they will select us.

The estimates of amounts required for the public service and the payments authorized by parliament will be laid before you. These will include an appropriation for the work of the royal commission on government organization which has been recently established to recommend improvements in the organization and methods of operation of the departments and agencies of the government which it thinks will best promote efficiency, economy and improved service in the dispatch of public business.
This commission is commonly referred to as a Hoover-type commission along the lines of the Hoover commission which was so active across the border for a period extending over many years. I notice that in the immigration branch the minister is asking for a total of $13,294,321. This amount exceeds last year's total by $448,507 and there may be supplementary estimates which will add to the increase in the forthcoming fiscal year. What I should like to know is whether the so-called Hoover-type commission has yet investigated the operations of the immigration branch and if it has not whether the minister expects such an examination of this branch of her department to take place at an early date.
I do not have the statistics here but the number of immigrants now being allowed into Canada is only about half of what it was a number of years ago, and I wonder how the decline in the number of immigrants has been reflected in the annual amounts asked for by the immigration branch. When you divide the total of $13 million by some
100,000	proposed immigrants you arrive at
1942	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration an overhead cost for the immigration branch approximating $130 for every man, woman and child and in the case of a family of five, which I am sure is a normal household, would run to $650. This seems like an extraordinarily high overhead.
I notice that there are some 2,000 employees in the branch and 100,000 immigrants divided by 2,000 means that the average immigration officer, if he alone is involved in the processing of an application, is only able to accomplish the necessary work involved at the rate of one per week. I would not have the feeling, if I were an immigration official, that I was operating at the height of efficiency if I averaged only one immigrant each week. I should like to ask the minister, in the light of the fact that the number of immigrants was only half what it was in other years, has there been any drastic reduction in the amount of money requested for the operation of the branch. I should like to refer the minister also to another matter and to ask her for a report. I regret that I shall have to be out of the committee for about one hour, but I hope the minister will not forget and I can see the reply in Hansard if the reply is given during that hour. I noticed when the Prime Minister was speaking on the bill of rights on July 1, 1960 and as recorded at page 5646 of Hansard for that date-this is the only reference to what I am about to say that I can easily find but there were others which were even more distinct-the Prime Minister said:
Mr. Speaker, that is very necessary. There will be some statutes in existence which will have to be changed and which will be interpreted accordingly.
The Prime Minister left an understanding with this house that if the bill of rights became law every order in council that existed at that time, every item of legislation that was in existence and every item of regulation of the various ministries would have to be carefully reviewed in order to ensure that they complied with the spirit and intent of the bill of rights. I believe the minister has continually denied that any of the regulations of her department violate the bill of rights. We have contended that these regulations are based, in part at least, on racial discrimination. I should like the minister to indicate at this time whether the regulations of the department have yet been reviewed by some department or officer of the government to ensure that they do not continue to violate the intent and spirit of the bill of rights that was enacted last year.


I am asking the minister in effect, therefore, whether her department has been submitted to the Hoover-type commission for scrutiny and whether any of the regulations, in particular, have yet been submitted to some department or officer of government to ensure that they comply with the provisions of the bill of rights.

Perhaps inasmuch as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has indicated that he will not be in the committee I might answer his questions now. To take the last one first, I think he would agree with me that it was new orders and acts which were to be reviewed by the Minister of Justice. I understand that any alleged variance with the spirit of the bill of rights or letter of the bill of rights is to be decided by the courts. In so far as existing legislation is concerned, we are taking a very hard look at it ourselves. I might add that that is one of the things that is holding up the introduction of the new act. We are being very careful indeed to make sure we do nothing that would in any way run contrary to either the letter or the spirit of the bill of rights.
Now with reference to the increase of $448,500 which my hon. friend noted, I might tell him that $410,000 of this is the result of increases in wages and salaries. If he will refer to the details on pages 144 to 151 he will find therein the notation that we actually, within those votes, have one less employee than we had previously. As he knows, however, there have been pay increases during the past year which have necessitated this additional amount of money.
It is impossible to break down the costs of immigration according to the number of immigrants who are landed because, in addition to those who come into this country as immigrants there are many people who come as visitors. All of these people have to be examined. There are businessmen coming into this country all the time. There are returning Canadian citizens, and there are 58 million border crossings. All of these people have to pass through the hands of the immigration department. It is, therefore, clearly improper to try to divide the number of landed immigrants into the cost and say that costs are rising because there are fewer immigrants and there is an increase in the cost of administration.
We have been very careful to keep the costs at a minimum. I do feel that if the costs could be broken down completely having regard not only to salaries and wages but the efforts of others which require remuneration, it would be found that the actual costs

have decreased. What increases there are- with the exception of Indian affairs-are entirely reflected in increases in salaries and wages, a matter over which we have no control departmentally. I think those were the only matters brought up by my hon. friend.
He has referred to the commission which is headed by Mr. Glassco. I can tell him that the deputy minister has been called to testify before this commission and we have been in communication with them. I do not believe for a moment that their investigation of the affairs of our department is at an end, in fact I think they have just touched the surface. We are most happy to co-operate with them. After all, this is a sizable department with some 5,000 employees. We are just as anxious as anyone else to see it streamlined to the extent possible consistent with proper service to the public.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks on this department will be very brief because I believe that the policy being followed by the department is very sensible and humane. I am really prompted to rise because of what I consider to be the rather incredible position taken by the Liberal party during this debate. It shows a complete lack of consistency or cohesion, just as is the case in so many other departments with which we deal. They have been up so many times complaining about unemployment in the country, and during those debates they profess to have great faith in what is said by the Canadian Labour Congress, which speaks for organized labour in this country.
However when something else seems to be politically expedient during the course of another debate, when they feel there might be some other group of voters to whom they could appeal, they take an entirely different course. Both the hon. member for Cartier and the hon. member for Fort William have complained about the reduction in immigration. They have complained, too, that the minister has said she has tried to discourage certain types of immigrant, particularly during the wintertime when jobs are rather scarce. I should like to bring to the attention of the committee what the Canadian Labour Congress has put forth as the official position of labour with regard to immigration. I think it should be put on Hansard. This is a memorandum to the government of Canada, dated January 22, 1959, and I am quoting from page 34 of that document:
So far as the number of immigrants to be admitted is concerned, this cannot be as readily solved by using any one arbitrary figure. Obviously the figure that is good for one year may not be
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration good for another. We are in agreement with the general economic immigration policy that the flow of immigrants should be regulated by the country's absorptive capacity. We agree further that to bring in immigrants during a period of high unemployment is to do an injustice both to the immigrants and to Canadian citizens who are looking for and unable to find work. As we have said before, organized labour is not opposed to immigration but it is opposed to bringing in immigrants when there are no jobs for them except at the expense of Canadian workers.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: That is exactly what I said last night.

not think the views that are being expressed by the Liberal party are going to be very popular. It is not a selfish thing I am suggesting but rather it is a humane thing to curtail immigration at times of unemployment and particularly during the winter. I am not suggesting it only as a protection for Canadian workers; I think it is a completely inhuman policy to bring in immigrants when there is no work for them and when it may result in such a struggle for them. We have had that experience too. We can recall that in 1956, when a period of unemployment quite evidently was approaching, the largest number of immigrants were brought in that had ever been brought into this country in one year and that action no doubt added to the great difficulties with which we were faced at that time. Subsequently, many of those people were faced with a good deal of hardship because they could not find employment and they were obliged to make their way back to their own countries.
I think it is quite clear that in suggesting some of these measures that have been taken to curtail immigration at times and for specific purposes, there is nothing selfish in any way about it but that it is actually as much for the protection of those who would come here as immigrants as for any other reason. Certainly as the country is able to absorb immigrants I am sure that all parties and all members of the house and the people of the country will want to welcome just as many as possible. Many of the various nationalities that have come here have made great

I should like to reply immediately, Mr. Chairman, to some of the things that were said by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and I will deal first with the last thing he said. He talked about the number of immigrants brought into this country in the year 1956. I can tell the hon. gentleman that as to the immigrants that were brought in, the records of the department as well as statements made by the acting minister in 1957, which appear in Hansard in reply to questions and everything else will show that the immigrants who were brought in in the year 1956 had no difficulty whatsoever in finding employment. In fact in the winter of 1956-57 there was not even the normal amount of seasonal unemployment in this country and no restriction was put on the movement of immigrants that winter; in fact the situation was quite the reverse.
What is more, the unemployment figures which have often been given for the month of June, 1957, when the previous government went out of office, indicate quite clearly that the level of unemployment was so low that it was what is usually regarded as full employment. Therefore, these statements that have been made are completely and entirely at variance with the facts that have been placed on the records by members of the present administration since they took office and before they realized the situation was changing.
It is true that after the beginning of 1958, when there was a good deal of unemployment, instead of trying to deal with the problem as they should have done and as it was their duty to do, members of the government from the Prime Minister down tried to find someone else to blame for unemployment and they have been doing that ever since. But I might remind the hon. gentleman that in the 1957 election campaign the Prime Minister was so unaware of the fact that immigration was causing unemployment that he promised to triple the immigration which the Liberals were carrying on at that time, as shown by a quotation put on the record by the hon. member for Fort William.
Of course, the Prime Minister was rather selective with regard to the localities in which he made these statements. He made them mostly to people at ethnic organizations and to their organizations but he did not go out and make them in the rural parts of Ontario where some of his friends were going around


and complaining about what the previous government had done in the great crisis in Austria in 1956, the great Hungarian movement which, as the hon. lady pointed out last year when I asked her a question, had been an entirely successful effort. When I asked her a question she pointed out that so few of these Hungarian immigrants, most of whom came out without anything except the clothes on their back, have need of help from the government that no separate statistics were being kept of the number.

The hon. gentleman now says that they put Canadians out of work. The minister did not say that in the speech she made in Winnipeg that was quoted by the hon. member for Fort William a few minutes ago.
The other thing that touched me particularly about the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, who talks about one Liberal expressing one set of views and another Liberal expressing another set of views, is this. He obviously did not consult with his neighbour the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. Had he done so he would have found out, unless that hon. gentleman is talking differently from the way in which he talked a short time ago, that this was a brutal, inhumane department staffed with bureaucrats who were not fit to be in the public service. That is how that hon. gentleman got into this House of Commons, namely by the most shocking misrepresentation of a situation which the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway knows very well and which provided a legacy that the hon. lady was obliged to deal with somewhat later.
The hon. gentleman talks about their being difference of view in the Liberal party. Of course there are differences of view in the Liberal party and we are not ashamed of those differences of view. However, there is no difference of view about this one basic fact namely that immigration is necessary for the healthy growth and development of this country. But you must have the two things proceeding hand in hand, namely the growth and the immigration.
A proper and well worked out immigration policy can contribute to growth. But if the growth does not take place, confidence is destroyed. If there is a depressed condition in the country it will be impossible, whatever immigration policy there is, to attract immigrants to the country because whatever one may or may not think desirable, immigrants seeking work are not going to come to a country in which there is not any work. I do not think anyone would argue

about that statement at all. Our view is that the sooner we get back to a government that knows how to administer this country and its finances, to restore order with regard to business and employment and to get back growth once more, the sooner we shall have healthy immigration. Until we do the one, we shall not have the other.

There was-as I think the hon. member for Fort William said-the largest influx since 1913. It was about twice as much as the average in the last 10 or 15 years. I claim no credit for the views which have been expressed by more than one economist to the effect that when you have a year in which you have a tremendous influx for one reason or another, you thereafter have a digestive process which goes on for a period of time. This is because, as is obvious, the motivation for the abnormal influx brought with it many immigrants who in the normal course of planning would have come in subsequent years, but for reasons which might be personal, which might be economic or otherwise, they accelerated their plans in order to take advantage of certain circumstances or avoid others and consequently came perhaps two or three years ahead of the time they had normally planned to come.
In the subsequent period, of course, those persons were already in Canada and the ones who were left formed the retinue of the group that had come originally in the boom year. That is the only explanation I can offer, other than that in the subsequent years of course, in so far as Europe is concerned, we all know that economic conditions were very bright,
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration other conditions were favourable, and people do not move away from what is to them a satisfactory condition.
Despite that we have had respectable numbers coming out to Canada. I do not lay claim to any great success in the matter of numbers. I will say that we have not encouraged people to come forward who had little chance of settling in Canada without difficulty. It would not be fair to them; it is not fair to the Canadians who are here.
I think the original explanation of the great influx resulting in a digestive process for two or three years is coupled with the economic condition of Europe and is quite likely the answer to the question.

1946	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration while they are here without engaging in either full or part-time employment.
There has been some misunderstanding with reference to the seeking of employment by some of these students. If the employment which the student seeks is in line with his course of study, if it is something that contributes to the education which he is seeking, such as internship in the case of doctors, or possibly work in a library in the case of a person pursuing that type of course, and if that employment does not take a job away from a Canadian who is dependent upon it for his livelihood, then the student is granted permission to accept that employment.
This is far removed from the student who is possibly taking a pre-med course and goes out and takes a job driving a truck, thereby putting some truck driver out of a job. This is the type of thing we try to avoid. I hope I am making myself clear. If the employment is in line with his course of study, he is granted permission to take it.
However, we must come back to the original condition under which he came into the country, and that is that he had attested to the fact that he had sufficient funds to maintain himself and to pay his fees during the course of study.

The operation of this system has left a good deal of spare time on the hands of American farmers who, it must be remembered, have a lot of money invested in machinery. The letter reads in part as follows:
The suggestion is not new.
I pointed that out last night. I continue:
It has been put forward several times since the national employment service was established and it has been reviewed and discussed on various occasions.
Speaking historically, the department charged with the responsibility for immigration has always been responsible for the satisfactory establishment of immigrants in Canada, including their placement, as required. The immigration branch of this department is responsible for the implementation of government policy on immigration and the functions of the branch in this respect include: programming; recruiting, counselling; documentation; reception; distribution and placement; establishing the admissibility of immigrants; developing

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration settlement opportunities in rural areas as well as urban centres; and establishment of selfemployed persons.
Reception is one of the most important phases in the implementation of the Canadian immigration policy. A dissatisfied immigrant, in addition to the problems he may cause in Canada, may through his letters home frustrate our future immigration prospects. Successful immigrants are our most important recruiting factors.
Initial placement is an essential part of the reception of the imigrant who is in need of services which are not generally provided to other Canadian residents through a government agency, i.e., locating temporary accommodation, financial assistance while awaiting employment, arrangements with employers to make advances of salary to meet the migrant's initial needs, explanation of immigrants' background and training to employers, interpreter services, etc. It is important for the immigrants to know that they have a service of the government to turn to in time of need for they are not, like other residents in Canada, aware of the multiplicity of services made available, and it would create confusion, disappointment and hardship if upon arrival they had to consult with several of the agencies of governments in Canada.
One important aspect is that a significant portion of the immigrants come to Canada to establish themselves in small businesses or on farms. The immigration branch has a program of guidance and counselling for these cases. Such immigrants are placed in employment which will acquaint them with Canadian methods of operation, marketing and buying practices, before they embark on their own enterprises. These cases are followed up by the immigration officers at regular intervals, and at the appropriate time the immigrants are given the proper counselling which permits them to establish their own business or purchase their own farm. One important factor of this phase of the immigration program is the relation of friendship and trust between the immigrants and the immigration officers.
It is not the department's policy to accept responsibility for the placement of immigrants who have been in Canada for more than a year. However, officials of the national employment service have been informed that they may always, if they so wish, refer problem cases to the immigration branch. This department is also responsible to assist indigent immigrants until they are eligible for municipal and provincial welfare benefits up to a period of one year after their arrival in Canada. It seems normal therefore that the officers of the immigration branch should make the necessary effort to place those who are unemployed instead of providing them with financial assistance.
The question of duplication between the immigration branch and the national employment service and the possibility of financial saving was considered in 1955 by the treasury board on instructions of the then minister of finance. It was established that if the immigration branch were to cease to look after the initial placement of immigrants this would not result in any financial saving, as the immigration branch must retain its staff to carry out other essential immigration services. The conclusion was reached that this service was essential to the reception of the immigrants and should remain as a function of the immigration branch.
Notwithstanding the importance of the placement service of the immigration branch in the reception of immigrants, it remains a fact that they are encouraged wherever possible to use the facilities of the national employment service and this is a general practice followed by immigration

officers. In this connection the excellent co-operation received by the immigration branch from the national employment service must be acknowledged.
I think that describes the situation very-well in so far as the thinking of the department is concerned.

I personally went with him to see the minister's officer. He said, "We do not expect immigrants from the United Kingdom to ask for assistance, they are expected to have enough stability and so on to stand on their own feet". I was present when that was said. I will supply the minister with the full details.
As a matter of fact, this immigrant was a senior official in the immigration service of Great Britain when he came to this country and he had recommendations of the highest kind from the colonel of his regiment and from the British ministry that had charge of the department for which he worked. That is one particular instance of which I have knowledge. It took place some year or two ago. I have had the matter brought to my attention a number of times by a number of immigrants.
This is the only case of which I can speak from personal experience because I went to the immigrant concerned. As a consequence, he was able to borrow sufficient funds from Great Britain and returned to
Great Britain. He was a man of excellent education, and had given excellent service to the commonwealth and had fought for the things we believe in. However, he was obliged to return to Great Britain because he was denied two or three months assistance to tide him over a rocky period after he had suffered a series of most unfortunate experiences. I bring that matter to the minister's attention. I will look up the file and give her the details. If my memory serves me correctly, this incident took place during the administration of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

Citizenship-
48. Citizenship registration branch, $845,871.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to make one or two observations about this item. The citizenship registration branch is, of course, concerned with persons who have come here as immigrants in main, although not all of them are in that category; some are returning Canadians who want to have their citizenship restored. Except in one respect it is largely simply a great registry in the department here in Ottawa. But since 1954 or 1955- I ought to remember the year but I am not quite sure of it-the department has set up a number of citizenship courts in various parts of the country because we found that there were such concentrations when I was in office-and the minister has found this situation also-in a number of places, such concentrations of potential citizens in certain places that the local county courts or their equivalent in the other provinces could not handle the volume of traffic. I think it would be interesting to have for the last two years the global figures of the number of persons who have become citizens in each of these areas, and any other observations the minister would like to make about this situation; that is, whether there are any other places where there is a backlog.
One thing that always interested me when I was minister was that I managed to make a reasonable profit for the treasury on the operations in Toronto, and even in Montreal. I wonder whether the minister, being an accountant, has a balance sheet for all the courts and can say whether the fee is sufficient to pay the full cost of these courts.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Most of these courts have not been in operation long enough for us to have decided that. I might also say that the primary purpose for the establishment of the courts, in so far as I am concerned, is to have uniform treatment rather than making money. It stands to reason that we do not intend to open courts in areas where traffic does not warrant it. However, I do have a small statement here and possibly it will answer some of the questions I have been asked.
During the calendar year 1960 courts of Canadian citizenship were opened in London, Ontario; Winnipeg, Manitoba; Edmonton, Alberta and Vancouver, British Columbia. In addition we have in this current calendar year appointed a court of Canadian citizenship in Moncton, New Brunswick. This brings to eight the number of courts of Canadian citizenship now in operation. I might also add that it is hoped to open a court of Canadian citizenship in Ottawa later this year. It is also planned to hold a meeting of

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
the presiding officers of these courts in the near future to help them to arrive at a more uniform system in dealing with applicants for Canadian citizenship.
To date the complete statistical returns on the granting of certificates of Canadian citizenship are not available. However, it appears that there will be a slight decrease from last year in the number of persons who have applied for and been granted Canadian citizenship. Information available for the first three quarters of 1960 shows that 46,000 persons were granted Canadian citizenship compared with 49,000 for the same period in 1959.
During these same periods the number of certificates of Canadian citizenship and miniature certificates of Canadian citizenship issued to persons who are already Canadian citizens has decreased from 32,381 in the first three quarters of 1959 to 31,542 in the first three quarters of 1960. Of course, that is not much of a decrease. The issue of the miniature certificates of Canadian citizenship continued to be the more popular during 1960.
The total revenue from all sources for the branch for the calendar year 1960 amounts to $327,623. This is mainly from the operations of the courts of Canadian citizenship.
To answer my hon. friend's question, in 1960 the court in Toronto had 9,686 applications; Montreal had 5,871; Hamilton had 1,995; London, which was only opened May 1, had 453; Moncton of course has just opened; Winnipeg, which opened on October 3, had 288; Edmonton, opened October 18, had 205; and Vancouver, which opened August 15, had 798. So I think it will be another year or so before we can really properly assess the traffic and the expenses of the courts. But I am sure that with the amount of money that has come in during the past year we certainly will not be operating at a loss. For 1961-62 we forecast about $427,500 altogether.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, reverting to the claim of the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate as to a profit made on these courts when he was minister, does the minister, who is an accountant, know whether in fact the claim of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who is not an accountant, is valid?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: I did not audit his accounts, but I would be willing to attest to the fact that in so far as the records of the department show, he is quite correct.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
There is one problem that the minister knows has been quite troublesome. There is a great incentive, of course, for persons of foreign nationality to seek to become Canadian citizens because that is the 90205-6-124
way in which they get the franchise in this country. But British subjects who emigrate to Canada have only to be here a year and they get the franchise without becoming Canadian citizens. Therefore they-at least, I say "therefore"; I am not imputing motives to anyone in the house-presumably have less incentive to seek citizenship than persons of foreign nationality. In fact, the records did show up until the last time I checked them that these British subjects did not become Canadian citizens in quite the same number. Has there been any improvement in that respect in the past year?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: I could not really say there has been. I wish I could report that there had been an improvement, because I think these people should become Canadian citizens. But apart from encouraging them whenever we run into them, I do not think there is very much else we can do. I have just been reminded of something that I should have mentioned. In the current year we are producing a film which we hope will be some encouragement to them.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
I can understand the viewpoint of the minister in wishing to encourage uniformity and perhaps a standard ceremony in the application or the granting of papers of citizenship. However, I would like to ask the minister whether any thought has been given to a rather serious aspect on the other side of the picture. I have reference to people who have been here the required five years and who have made the required application, but who come from a country whereby almost by nature they have a temperament of being high-strung, emotional and excitable.
From my own personal experience I know people who have been good citizens and in my estimation they are entitled to citizenship. On many occasions I had visited them in their homes. I can sit down and talk to them and they can talk to me. I understand them; they understand me. I have actually sponsored some of these people. But immediately they get in the courtroom, with the judge up on the bench and the spectators all around, they freeze. Their mind goes blank; they are back to the language and the customs of the country from which they came.
Although I have been speaking to them for perhaps two years in English, right then and there they do not know English; they cannot understand it; they cannot speak it. I have seen that happen. I know it happened only recently in Vancouver. I know of cases in the interior of exactly the same thing. As a matter of fact I drew one to the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration attention of the deputy minister and he was very, very kind about it. This does happen.
Is consideration given to that situation, to this emotionalism and blankness which under those circumstances overcomes these people? I think we know it. I think the majority of us, if we have to face even a traffic charge, have a feeling of nervousness when we go before the judge. Therefore I think it is understandable and I think it is important that something be done to help these people.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
This is, of course, a recognized human failing. This is one of the reasons we want to have these courts wherever possible, because we can speak to our own presiding officers; we can draw these matters to their attention and plead for their tolerance and understanding.
If the applicant comes before the county court judge-I make no aspersions on his motives-it is true that we cannot speak to that judge because we have no jurisdiction whatsoever over him. I may say, however, that the applicant is not judged entirely on what happens to him in court. We do have a pre-examination and I think it has been our experience in our own courts that by the time the applicant comes to court he has had such friendly relationships with the staff of the court and has received such kindness from them that to some extent he loses his fear. We hope he loses all his fear. It stands to reason he is going to be excited. His enunciation in repeating the oath may not be as clear as we would expect of a Canadian but I am sure we are gradually overcoming these difficulties and we hope we shall overcome them completely.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: It did seem to me strange, having in mind the number of immigrants and the population of various places, that Calgary should not have been included in that list.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: We have a court in Edmonton. I am not sure what we are going to do, but we did not consider there was sufficient traffic to make it worth while having one court in Edmonton and another in Calgary. In some of these places we have in mind making a travelling court out of the existing court. Courts will be held at intervals in different places in the same area.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to emphasize the point made by my colleague the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. There is a great deal of confusion in Alberta with respect to this court in Edmonton. There is a feeling it is a temporary court. There is a feeling that someone from Medicine Hat might have to go to Edmonton to appear

before it, and I suggest to the hon. lady, whom we all admire, that it might be well to clear up this situation.
I have another question to raise and it has to do with refusal to grant citizenship. I am thinking at the moment of one individual of central European birth who has a European name. He has applied continually for citizenship and his application has been approved by the district court, but when his file comes to Ottawa he has been refused. I have been told by the registrar that the reason for refusal is a secret. I feel that as a member of parliament I am entitled to some confidence. I am not going to betray it. But on behalf of this man's sponsors and on behalf of the court in Medicine Hat who are most interested in this man I should like to know why he should continually apply, continually pay a $10 fee and continually be refused. It seems to me that that is not Canadian. If the man has some mark against him, should not some of us know what that mark is?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: There are some aspects of this type of case which cannot be divulged but if my hon. friend would like to bring his specific case before me I should be very glad to have a look at it and I will tell him what I can tell him, in any event.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: Can the minister give the approximate date when the citizenship court will be established in Ottawa, and will she indicate the field of its jurisdiction? Over what other counties in eastern Ontario would it have jurisdiction in addition to the historic county of Carleton?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: I am afraid I shall have to leave that question for the time being because it has several facets. We have an allotment for it in next year's estimates so I hope we shall get it open during the current calendar year.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to express appreciation to the minister and to the officials of her department for what they have done in connection with the appointment of what I might term ad hoc judges in districts far removed from places where the courts usually sit. That has happened in the area of Fort Vermilion which is some 300 miles from Peace River where the nearest district court holds regular sittings. The arrangement has proved of great value. Frequently during the summer and fall when rivers cannot be crossed it is impossible to get down to these courts other than by air. The practice has proved very useful and I hope it will be increasingly followed.
I believe the minister advised me in her last letter that a member of the R.C.M.P.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
had been appointed there. That is all very well. I think they are an admirable body although I have had my differences with them professionally at various times. But they are frequently moved. Sometimes a constable is appointed to be an ad hoc judge. Then, he is moved and there is a vacancy. I would suggest that thought be given to making appointments of a more permanent nature; to choosing someone who is residing in the area for some time.
I should like to take this opportunity to make some reference to the observations of the hon. member for Vancouver East. I have appeared before the courts at different times for a quarter of a century. During that time in district courts I have heard many judges dealing with the applications of those who wish to become citizens of this country and I do not think I have come across one occasion in all that period when the judge concerned has not been sympathetic, courteous and considerate, careful to see that he has put these people at their ease. I am confident that the new courts and the judges appointed by the minister will continue that practice.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Following the question raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East with regard to applicants for citizenship, may I say that when they appear before the judge they usually get tongue-tied in answering questions. I have here in my hand a questionnaire with 41 questions on it which the judge asks the applicants in court. Needless to say, some of these questions are difficult even for Canadians to answer. I will read one or two as examples.
One question reads: What written document is the basis of the constitution of Canada? Another is: What is the name of the most recent act of parliament affecting our constitution? Another question is: Why is the Statute of Westminster important?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: How many school children, or even adult, could answer those?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Some of those questions are difficult for even Canadians to answer, let alone for these people who appear before a judge with a meagre knowledge of English. They become tongue-tied, unable to say a word, and are turned down. Once they are turned down they are asked to file another application within two years. That is accompanied by a request for another fee of $5. A situation of this kind is surely to be regretted, and some reasonable attitude should be taken by the judges when they examine these people. I have had several cases in my constituency; in fact they come up after every citizenship court. People come to me and say they could not get citizenship papers. They 90205-6-1241
got tongue-tied in court; yet they can speak to me, in broken English, it may be, but I can understand them very well.
Then there is the case of the man who may have lived in Canada for 20 years and who will never acquire a substantial knowledge of the English language. Yet he is a good citizen and has probably raised a family. He, and others like him, are unable to obtain citizenship papers simply because they cannot answer the questions which are asked of him.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, these questions do not emanate from this department. This must have been a list of questions compiled by the judge himself. In any event, I should inform the hon. member for Fort William that we do have text books which are made available to all applicants for citizenship. These text books answer most of these questions and certainly the ones the hon. member read off.
We think it is advisable that applicants for citizenship should know a little about the country. I agree with him that possibly some of our own Canadian citizens do not know this either but after all they were born here and were supposedly educated in this country and have probably forgotten much of what they learned in school as is the case with all of us.
With respect to long term residents and a lack of knowledge of the language, there is usually some leniency exercised by the judges in the cases of persons who have been here an extended length of time and who have not had an opportunity of learning one of Canada's two basic languages. I think of persons who have been here 20 years and who demonstrate that by reason of circumstances they have been unable to take language courses or to mingle with their neighbours to the extent of having acquired fluency in English or French. Such persons are usually given special treatment by the judge of the court.
Perhaps I may be permitted to relate to the committee an amusing incident that came to my own attention. A young lady of my acquaintance was taking a language course. She came to me with a book which I must admit was a product of my own department. She asked me what is a very small animal with six legs. I said I did not know. She was able to show me the question in the book: What is a very small animal with six legs? We got out the encyclopedia, the dictionary and some books on animals that I have, but we were unable to find an answer to the question.
With great glee I brought the question to my departmental officials and they were as much in the dark as I was. I believe the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration answer turned out to be an ant. I am sure none of the hon. members of this committee would consider an ant an animal but apparently in strict terms it is. However, if none of us could answer that question I am sure we can have every sympathy when a question of this nature is put to a person who is attempting to learn the English language.
The other side of that matter, of course, is that there was a book of instructions from which she could have secured the necessary information but in directing her studies the teacher had neglected to give her the book of instructions and had given her only the book containing the questions.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: I agree that there are books of instructions, Mr. Chairman, but often when these people appear before the judge, even though they know the answers to the questions, they cannot talk, become mute and are turned down. That is the difficulty. I wonder if the minister could instruct, advise, or suggest to the judges concerned that they use a little discretion in the matter.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: In February we are having our own presiding officers in and will be making some of these suggestions to them. I am sorry to inform the hon. member, that we cannot make suggestions to county court judges.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to know what the procedures are now when an applicant appears before a judge and has to answer possibly 48 questions. I can recall my own application for citizenship. Although there were 48 questions I am happy to say that we were supplied with 48 answers too.
