49. Citizenship branch, $808,322.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, because it is only a few minutes before five o'clock, perhaps I may be permitted to make a statement on this subject so that we could start next day from this point.
As I presented an outline of the continuing activities of the citizenship branch only eight months ago, I shall confine my remarks today to reporting on a few significant developments that have occurred since that time.
First of all, I should like to speak of language classes. Special language classes for newly landed immigrants, who would otherwise have to await the opening of the fall term, were made available in the summer in an increased number of centres. Notably popular and successful this year were the

classes organized for the first time in Winnipeg. In Toronto a publicity campaign conducted through spot announcements on radio in a variety of languages produced most gratifying results. Nearly 1,000 students enrolled in an intensive six-week course involving five evenings each week.
In the field of teacher training, a total of 45 teachers of immigrants attended the special summer course conducted by the Ontario department of education during July and August. At the instigation of the citizenship branch, arrangements were made between provincial governments for the first time to permit the attendance of nine supervisors and senior teachers from outside Ontario. The course, which is intended to improve the standards of instruction in language classes, is now well established and will be expanded somewhat this summer.
With the assistance of the branch, initial steps are now being taken to provide special courses for teachers of French to immigrants. The first of such courses will be held in Montreal the latter part of February.
A meeting is being planned by the branch for this summer of leading experts from the various provinces in the field of language and citizenship instruction for immigrants. The meeting will provide the first opportunity for such experts to exchange views and experiences and to discuss problems of mutual interest.
Increased efforts have also been made by the branch to promote the filing of citizenship applications by those eligible to do so. A series of advertisements have been run in the ethnic press. A poster on this subject was also prepared and, with the co-operation of the Post Office Department, displayed in all post offices throughout the country. Articles on the steps to citizenship and the advantages of acquiring citizenship were prepared for the use of ethnic newspapers across Canada.
In order to reach as many people as possible of those newcomers who, although eligible, have delayed in applying for Canadian citizenship, a film on the subject is now in process. It is intended for use with ethnic groups and voluntary organizations working with newcomers. The film will outline the factors involved in reaching such an important decision as changing allegiance, as well as the main court procedures.
At present, plans are being completed for a revised booklet to assist applicants for citizenship in preparing themselves for examination before the courts. It is anticipated that the new booklet will assist applicants and the courts, in achieving and maintaining a desirable standard in respect of citizenship examinations.

I would like to refer also to the work of the citizenship branch in the promotion of citizenship activities among Canadians generally. Last summer the branch concentrated its efforts on the organization of impressive and colourful Dominion day celebrations in a few major centres. I mention only two. Through the united efforts of civic government, business and industry, voluntary and ethnic organizations, Winnipeg had a most distinctive and successful program. In Ottawa events centred around parliament hill. Members will recall the trooping of the colour, the special carillon recitals, the sunset ceremony and the very moving citizenship ceremony over which I had the honour to preside. This year, along with the more formal observances, the branch is encouraging broader community participation in the Dominion day festivities, in gradual preparation for the celebrations that will take place during centennial year.
Two significant events with which the branch has been closely associated recently were a national Y.M.C.A. conference of young adults who met last summer to discuss the role of responsible Canadian citizenship in the next decade, and a conference sponsored by the home and school associations for community leaders in New Brunswick on the conditions of bicultural co-operation in the region.
Resolutions adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It being five o'clock the house will now proceed to the consideration of public and private bills, the former having precedence, pursuant to section 3 of standing order 15.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FINANCIAL STATEMENT

speakeroldname: Mr. E. J. Broome (Vancouver South) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FINANCIAL STATEMENT
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-16, to amend the Companies Act (financial statements).
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to amend the Companies Act so that if the foreign parent of a Canadian subsidiary is deemed to be under Canadian law a public company the Canadian subsidiary must also be classed as a public company. There are now 11 Canadian companies acts, one federal and ten provincial. Canadian law does not require private companies to publish financial statements and, among other things, a private company is one which has less than 50 shareholders. Public companies are required by the federal act to publish annual statements of income, expenditures, profit or loss, debts, assets, inventories and surpluses. On the other
Private Bills
hand, a wholly owned subsidiary of any company, whether foreign or Canadian, is considered under the law to be a single corporate person and therefore can qualify as a private company and will not have to make its financial statements public.
It can be argued with reason that the right granted to private companies to keep their financial affairs safe from public scrutiny was intended as a guarantee of privacy for natural, not corporate, persons. Wholly owned subsidiaries are ultimately owned by the shareholders of the parent company; if there are more than 50 shareholders of the parent company then it can be argued that there are more than 50 shareholders of the subsidiary. It would therefore be in the spirit of the law to require wholly owned subsidiaries to submit separate financial statements both to the Secretary of State and to their parent corporation. It is my contention that this is the spirit of the law but that the letter of the law does not say this.
The amendment proposed in the bill will, of course, only affect companies incorporated by an act of parliament, but if this parliament gives a lead in this direction I think the provincial acts will be changed accordingly in due course. These provincial acts are not exactly similar to the federal act but generally speaking they make the same distinction between private and public companies.
The Canadian-American committee sponsored by the national planning association of the United States and the private planning association of Canada has recently published a booklet entitled "Policies and Practices of United States Subsidiaries in Canada" written by John Lindeman and Donald Armstrong. Mr. John Lindeman has wide experience in the field of international economic affairs with the United States government and as a private economic consultant. He is the author of earlier studies on United States business performance abroad published by the national planning association, and he is currently a partner in International Economic Consultants, Incorporated, in Washington. Professor Armstrong has had broad experience as an economic consultant in Canada and has recently been appointed director of the school of commerce at McGill University in Montreal.
The Canadian-American committee was established in 1957 to study problems arising from the growing interdependence between Canada and the United States. It has approximately equal representation from coast to coast. Its 60 members are business, labour, agricultural and professional leaders drawn in equal numbers from the United States and Canada. The committee was founded to foster

Private Bills
good relations between Canada and the United States and to study any problems which are in the common interests of both countries.
The booklet deals with the sale of equity stock in subsidiaries to Canadians, the use of Canadian personnel in these subsidiaries, how well or how badly such subsidiaries contribute to charity and education, and one chapter deals with the subject of the bill, that is, the publication of financial data of such subsidiaries. On page 46 the authors state as follows:
Complaints have come from financial, academic and professional sources that the failure of so many foreign owned companies to publish financial data imposes a factual blackout for them over much of the economy, and thus inhibits research. An analyst examining a problem of the concentration of industry, for example, will have much more difficulty studying the problem in Canada than would a student of the same problem in the United States or England. Even civil servants do not always have access to the financial data of individual companies. An economist in the Department of Trade and Commerce or in the Bank of Canada, who might be trying to assess the significance of a sample survey made of a particular industry, would have access to no more individual financial company data than would anyone else. Under existing rules, the information made available to the income tax division or the dominion bureau of statistics is not generally available to any other government department on an individual company basis. Market analysts report difficulty in trying to assess the future of an industry or of the individual companies that do sell shares, since in some cases they lack sufficient data for comparing companies and have no way of putting together financial statistics for an industry as a whole.
These complaints, Mr. Speaker, are quite legitimate when you consider the degree of ownership and control of Canadian industry exercised by foreign corporations. As far as control is concerned, according to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects 95 per cent of our automobile industry, 84 per cent of our rubber industry, 51 per cent of our chemical industry, 68 per cent of our petroleum industry and 55 per cent of our mining industry are controlled by United States capital alone. In the booklet I have referred to previously this statement is made:
Today well over one quarter of all industry in Canada is controlled in the United States. In manufacturing the proportion is approximately one half, and in the primary mineral resource industries -mining, smelting and petroleum-United States ownership is close to two thirds of the total. These are dramatic figures.
No other industrialized country has such a large share of its industry controlled by concerns beyond its border. By comparison foreign investment in the United States reached a peak before world war I but it only amounted to the equivalent of 15 per cent of the United States gross national product. As of today, foreign investment in the United States is down to 3 per cent of

the gross national product. On the other hand, foreign investment in Canada is now almost 61 per cent of the Canadian gross national product.
It almost seems fantastic, Mr. Speaker, that in so many areas of government legislation the cards have been stacked against companies which are either wholly Canadian or have Canadian participation. For example, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in his recent budget has corrected the situation which gave a tax advantage to foreign companies which would not permit any Canadian participation, and penalized foreign subsidiaries which did allow Canadian participation. The budget has eliminated this advantage and removed one barrier to further Canadian participation in these foreign owned subsidiaries.
This bill attempts to amend the Companies Act so that wholly owned subsidiaries of foreign companies will not be able to operate in secrecy but will have to publish the same financial information required of Canadian companies, and the same information which is required of foreign subsidiaries which have some Canadian participation. For instance, the royal commission on price spreads in food products, in its report dated September, 1959, page 52, recommended that private companies be required by law to publish the same information as public companies of their financial operations. The commission stated that information on the operation of the Canadian economy is necessary to the proper conduct of public affairs. They felt that if this information were available it would be a corrective to some of the abuses they found in the food industry. The royal commission on Canada's economic prospects in their final report at page 393, made the following recommendations:
(1)	wherever possible, such concerns should employ Canadians in senior management and technical positions,-
They are here referring to foreign owned subsidiaries.
-should retain Canadian engineering and other professional and service personnel, and should do their purchasing of supplies, materials and equipment in this country;
(2)	they should publish their financial statements and make full disclosure of the results of their Canadian operations;
(3)	they should include on their boards of directors a number of independent Canadians and they should sell an appreciable interest in their equity stock to Canadians.
The subject matter of another bill which I will be introducing, Mr. Speaker, will deal with the question of Canadian participation on the boards of directors of the companies. It is of note that the second recommendation of this royal commision is in line with the purpose of this bill.

It is interesting to note also that in the United Kingdom wholly owned subsidiaries are required by law to publish financial statements. Vauxhall, which is a General Motors subsidiary in the United Kingdom, regularly publishes complete details of its financial operations. According to the press there has been over the past five years a major flow of United States capital into the United Kingdom in order to build branch plants to service that market. It would seem, therefore, that foreign capital is not too concerned about this requirement, but is quite willing to take advantage of the fact there is no requirement so long as we are willing to give this advantage.
In the Canadian-American booklet to which I referred before I find that the authors interviewed some 150 officials of United States parent companies with subsidiaries in Canada and the operations of more than 50 United States companies operating in Canada. They state that most of the professional and governmental officials interviewed in Canada were firmly convinced that wholly owned subsidiaries should publish these financial statements. On the basis of these interviews they found that the management of most of the wholly owned United States subsidiaries in Canada had no strong opposition to the publication of the financial data in the detail now required of public companies. Incidentally it is well to note here that the data required under Canadian law is neither as extensive nor as detailed as that required under United States law, and which is furnished by the parent corporations of these same subsidiaries. The authors have come to the conclusion that the reason more of these wholly owned subsidiaries do not publish statements must be attributed more to inertia than any strong desire to keep their financial results away from public scrutiny. If this is so, then only through government legislation can we bring about this result.
In the Ottawa Journal of January 18 there was an interesting editorial referring to a speech made by Mr. Kennedy when he was given an honorary degree by the University of New Brunswick. In speaking about Canada-United States relations, Mr. Kennedy said:
It would be a pity to rigidify the Canadian economy merely for the sake of breaking lances with a phantom American colonialism. In return, American businessmen with substantial investments in Canada should be required by the dictates of self-preservation, if not simple equity, to increase the participation of Canadian money and personnel in the development of Canadian resources.
I would suggest, in the light of that statement, that Mr. Kennedy would be in agreement with the principle of this bill.
This bill was introduced for the first time in 1959 and was debated in this house. The

government, through the speech from the throne, has indicated that there will be measures relating to this problem. These measures may very well cover a wider field than can be covered in this bill. As I stated before, this bill simply amends the federal act and has no amending effect on any of the provincial companies acts. 1 do suggest, however, that if the bill when first introduced had been sent to a committee for study much valuable information would now be in the hands of the officials who have the job of drafting the proposed legislation. I suspect that these same officials will be referring to the debate which took place on this bill at that time as well as to the debate which I have just initiated.

It arrived only two days ago as far as my own post office box is concerned. I want to say that it is without doubt one of the finest and most exhaustive of the studies that have been made by responsible people and a responsible organization into the matter of the policies and the practices of United States subsidiaries in Canada. To those who may at this moment feel that there are objections to the bill may I say that if

Private Bills
they were to read this publication I feel they will find that all their objections are met, answered and disposed of.
In addition, of course, there is the positive approach in this exhaustive analysis, and that is the reason why this information should be available to the Canadian government and to the Canadian people. In my own reading of this pamphlet I was most interested to note the conclusion that the reason for the nonpublication of statements by the wholly owned subsidiaries was very simple, namely that the Canadian law does not require it. That was the major reason given by all those who were interviewed: As the Canadian law does not require it, why do it? However I was most interested to note that all those who were interviewed in the main stated that they could see no valid objection to the filing of such a return, that there was no reason at all why it should not be done and that it would not be very difficult to do. But why do it if the Canadian law does not require it?
However, one answer given as contained in this pamphlet put forward an objection and stated why at least two of the large companies did not want to have a Canadian law under which they would be obliged to file their financial statements and to give information as to their Canadian operations. The answer given by these two large concerns in Canada but wholly owned in the United States was this. First, there was the approach of one executive who objected to the publication of financial data on the ground that labour unions would be provided with information, and he did not want labour unions to be provided with information with regard to the operations of his company in Canada. Here is a company using our resources, our country and our labour and profiting by being allowed to operate in our country. But this executive did not want the men who do the work or their organizations known as trade unions to know about the financial affairs of his company. The reason he gave for this stand, as quoted by the authors of this most valuable pamphlet which I have mentioned, was that if the workers knew how much money the company was making it might make it difficult for the company in negotiations with the union with regard to improving the conditions of the workers. I think it is disgraceful that an executive of a company with an attitude like that should be allowed to continue without being obliged to make this information available.
On the other side of the picture, something that was also extremely interesting, was the approach of an executive of another company who did not want to be obliged to issue any financial statement or information because,

if that were done, the workers might want to unionize and he did not want them to unionize.
I think that this is a rather remarkable approach and that it is one we should consider. I believe that almost every argument definitely should be in favour of making it obligatory for these companies operating in Canada but owned outside of Canada to make public their operations, their financial status, their profit or loss and their depreciation.
The only other thing that I should like to add, Mr. Chairman, is the result of all the interviews that were undertaken by these two most responsible men, one from the United States and one from Canada, who did the research and the writing on behalf of this joint United States-Canada committee. This was their conclusion, and I think it should be noted. As a result of all their consultations with management and with executives and with many companies they were forced to the conclusion that, if it was felt in Canada that there should be the publishing of these financial statements, by far the vast majority of these companies would have no objection to doing so. If that is the conclusion, or the reaction, namely that fundamentally they have no objection to doing it but they are not doing it because it is not Canadian law, then I think that the hon. member who sponsored this bill has done the correct and proper thing in introducing legislation to make it Canadian law that these companies in the future will be obliged to operate in the same way as does any other company in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to follow the two distinguished members from British Columbia; I refer to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome), I am also happy to observe that all is calm in the province of British Columbia because on this occasion they seem to be in agreement.
Before going into the merits of the bill I think we should ask one question and then endeavour to answer it. The question is this: Why file a financial return at all? In order to answer that question I think one must look at the legal foundation of a corporation and see why some companies file financial returns and must do so under the law and why some companies do not file financial returns.
There are two distinct types of corporation. One is a private corporation and the other is a public corporation. Some are incorporated under the federal law, depending on their aims and objectives, and some are incorporated under the provincial law depending

on their aims and objectives. Of course, to determine whether it is a private corporation or a public corporation two points are involved. One is the number of shareholders and the other is how the stock is sold. If it is a private company it must have less than 50 shareholders. If it is a public company, it can be larger. Of course, the public then invests its money and subscribes for its shares.
That brings me to the particular answer of the question: Why file a financial statement at all? The reason why this practice grew up is briefly this. When the public are subscribing for shares there is an obligation on the corporation and on the directors of the corporation which is a public corporation to file a financial report so that investors in this country and in other countries who are investing in a corporation in Canada may get a fair shake for their money.
I am one of those Canadians who believes that Canadians and other investors in this country should get a fair shake for their money. That is the principle behind filing a financial statement. I do not think it was ever anticipated, with the greatest respect to the two members for Vancouver, that the reason why-if I understood their remarks correctly-a financial statement is filed is to give some state control over any corporation.
I am one of those Canadians who is always a little sceptical when I see state control either over a corporation or an individual, because it leads me back to the feeling of what might be the manifesto of the socialists.

It would seem to me that if we are to do anything we should be very cautious not to kill any kind of business or any chance that capital may come in from the United States to Canada.
We have only to compare the economy of the province of Alberta over the last 30 years with that of the province of Saskatchewan to illustrate my point. In the province of Alberta we have not had control or regulation to any degree such as is suggested in this bill, and we have a very expansive enterprise. Therefore the government is able to budget each year eventually, because of the oil industry, to very much better advantage than is the socialist government of the province of Saskatchewan. As a result, we get better enterprise, better roads and everything that goes along with it. I am one of those people who would oppose any feeling or suggestion at any time of anti-Americanism in this country.
I am one of those who believe we should always encourage American or any other foreign capital to come into this country and develop our resources so that we can get full employment. There is always a lot of talk about this, that and the other, but the fact is that if business is healthy and making a profit, a man has a job and there is prosperity in this country. In that manner it seems to me we can get full employment.

Let us take the industrial development of the province of Saskatchewan and compare it with the province of Alberta. You have a greater degree of prosperity in that province. People flocked into Alberta, while they left Saskatchewan, and this is because of the capital pouring in from the United States.
